evidence_quotes.quote: Underperformance is not related to the ownership structure of water companies, but rather to poor regulatory design and lack of understanding of the regulatory requirements that are implicit in the management model chosen, namely the concession contract.

The methodology adopted is based on a micro-institutional analysis of the regulatory structure, according to the economic theory of water service regulation and on the empirical international literature which discusses the outcomes of alternative regulatory schemes.

The incidence of expenditure for WSS on the ﬁrst decile is currently 1.4%, one of the lowest in the Oecd (Oecd, 2010b, Oecd, 2011). The planned increase will bring this indicator at 1.98% on average, still in the lower range.
A recent survey conducted by Massarutto (2013), may help analyze the relative weight of these alternative possible explanations (Table 2).

The above described regulatory system has been deﬁned as “an incomplete contract dressed up as a gosplan” (Massarutto, 2011): while the (formal) deﬁnition, outlined in the law, describes a procedure based on the detailed ex-ante speciﬁcation of plans and obligations and trivializes regulation as mere veriﬁcation of compliance, its (actual) implementation implies a large number of discretional decisions to be taken, without any clear discipline.

criterion_notes.c1: Borderline/tangential: the paper's central focus is utility regulation, concession contracting, investment levels, and operator creditworthiness in the Italian WSS sector rather than household or community service access, although Section 3.3 and Table 2 briefly cite secondary national aggregate indicators for sanitation connection (69% to 76%), irregular supply (15% to 7%), and first-decile water expenditure share (1.4%).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain=yes) because it examines legal, institutional, and regulatory governance of Italy's 1994 WSS reform (Law 36/1994, ATOs/AATOs, Conviri, concession contracts, public/PPP/private delegation, and the MTN tariff-setting formula), but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (narrow=no) because these contractual, ownership, and tariff/cost-recovery rules are analyzed as determinants of operator cash-flow security, capital investment, and access to credit markets rather than as rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community service access. Note: even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the paper is still excluded due to lack of primary empirical evidence/methods (c3=no, E05).
criterion_notes.c3: No primary empirical evidence or systematic empirical synthesis. The paper is a narrative micro-institutional policy analysis and critique grounded in economic contract theory and secondary literature/reports (e.g., Massarutto 2013; OECD 2010b, 2011; Istat/CoNViRI), with no empirical data collection, qualitative fieldwork methods, econometric model, or systematic review protocol.
criterion_notes.c4: Unclear/secondary only: Section 3.3 and Table 2 reproduce national before/after summary figures from secondary sources on first-decile expenditure share (1.4%), irregular supply (15% to 7% nationally; 30% to 15% in the South), and connection to sanitation (69% to 76%), but the paper conducts no empirical measurement or analysis of household access outcomes, focusing instead on operator financial sustainability, investment curbing, and credit crunch.
criterion_notes.c5: No identifiable empirical study design, sampling frame, or analytical design linking an exposure to a household or community service access outcome; secondary macro-sector descriptive tallies of 95 ATOs and national reform indicators lack methodological specification.

study_design: Narrative micro-institutional and regulatory policy analysis / overview (non-empirical)
population_and_sample: Italian water supply and sanitation (WSS) sector across 95 optimal management areas (ATOs) described at the macro-sector level from secondary sources; no primary empirical sample reported
exposure: 1994 Italian WSS regulatory reform (compulsory territorial integration into ATOs, concession contracts, public/PPP/private delegation, Conviri/AATO regulators, and the MTN full-cost recovery tariff method)
outcome: Macro-sector utility financial sustainability, capital investment, and access to credit (with secondary national summary figures cited for tariff burden on the first decile, irregular supply, and sanitation connection)
rationale: Exclude as E05 (No empirical evidence). Massarutto and Ermano (2013) present a narrative micro-institutional policy critique of Italy's 1994 water and sanitation reform, drawing on economic regulation theory and secondary reports/working papers (e.g., Massarutto 2013; OECD 2010b, 2011; Istat/CoNViRI) without an empirical study design, primary data collection, qualitative socio-legal fieldwork, quantitative estimation, or systematic synthesis method. Moreover, under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, its institutional analysis examines how concession contracts, regulator structure (Conviri/AATOs), and the MTN pricing formula affect utility cash flows, investment levels, and operator creditworthiness rather than rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community service access; even under the plain Criterion 2 wording, it remains excluded for lack of empirical evidence.
